Appendix A A Log-Sobolev inequality and the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process
In this appendix we discuss known classical results for the reader’s convenience: we briefly review
the relationship between the
isoperimetric inequality for classical Fisher information,
the Log-Sobolev inequality, and
the rate of convergence to the fixed point for the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. These arguments were given by Carlen [25]
for a particular element of the two-parameter family of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Here we specialize to real-valued random variables, but allow arbitrary parameters in order to illustrate the parallels to the qOU semigroup. We also explicitly discuss the convergence to the fixed point,
which is only implicit in [25] but appears to be folklore.
Let  $f_{0}$  be a probability density on  $\mathbb{R}$  of a real-valued random variable  $X$ . The classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (cOU) process, for  $\theta>0$  and  $\sigma>0$  is given by the Fokker-Planck equation
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=\theta\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[xf\right]+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}={\mathcal{A}}_{\theta,\sigma^{2}}(f)\ .$
(176)
(Carlen considers the case where  $\theta=1$  and  $\sigma^{2}=1/\pi$ .)
The solution to this equation can be written (in terms of random variables) as
$\displaystyle X_{t}$
$\displaystyle=e^{-\theta t}X_{0}+\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\theta}}\sqrt{1-e^{-2\theta t}}Z\ ,$
(177)
where  $Z\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1)$  is an independent centered Gaussian random variable with unit variance. The stationary solution  $f_{\infty}$  therefore is a centered Gaussian distribution with variance  $\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)$ .
In particular, (177)
implies that the second moments satisfy
$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[X_{t}^{2}]$
$\displaystyle=e^{-2\theta t}\mathbb{E}[X_{0}^{2}]+(1-e^{-2\theta t})\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2\theta}\ .$
(178)
We use that the relative entropy
between a random variable  $X$  and a centered normal variable  $Z_{\sigma^{2}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2})$  is given by
$D(X\|Z_{\sigma^{2}})=-H(X)+\frac{1}{2}\log 2\pi\sigma^{2}+\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\mathbb{E}[X^{2}]$
as can be verified easily.
In particular, the relative entropy between the solution at time  $t$
and the fixed point  $Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)}$  is given by
$\displaystyle D(X_{t}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})$
$\displaystyle=-H(X_{t})+\frac{1}{2}\log\pi\sigma^{2}/\theta+\frac{\theta}{\sigma^{2}}\mathbb{E}[X_{t}^{2}]\ .$
(179)
Furthermore, we have the following de Bruijn-type identity:
Lemma 10.
Let  $\{X_{t}\}_{t\geq 0}$  be of the form (177), i.e., a solution to the cOU process.
Let
$J(X)=\int\frac{|\frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x}|^{2}}{f(x)}dx$
denote the Fisher information of a random variable  $X$  with distribution function  $f$ . Then
$\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}H(X_{t})$
$\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}J(X_{0})-\theta\ .$
(180)
Observe that the second summand essentially stems from the fact that
entropies transform very simply under rescaling of random variables, namely
$\displaystyle H(e^{-\theta t}X)=H(X)-\theta t\ .$
(181)
Eq. (181) significantly simplifies the analysis. Such a property does not hold in the quantum case: as a consequence, we do not have a simple expression in terms of  $J(X_{0})$  only.
Proof.
The derivative of the entropy along a semigroup with generator  ${\mathcal{A}}$  is given by the expression  $\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}H(e^{t{\mathcal{A}}}(f))=-\int{\mathcal{A}}(f)(x)\log f(x)dx$ . Using this fact gives
$\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}H(X_{t})$
$\displaystyle=-\theta\int\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}[xf(x)]\right)\log f(x)dx-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\int\frac{\partial^{2}f(x)}{\partial x^{2}}\log f(x)dx\ .$
(182)
Denoting  $f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x)$ , we obtain
$\displaystyle\int(xf)^{\prime}\log fdx$
$\displaystyle=-\int(xf)f^{\prime}/fdx=-\int xf^{\prime}dx=\int fdx=1\ ,$
(183)
where we have used partial integration and the fact that boundary terms vanish twice. Similarly,
we have
$\displaystyle\int f^{\prime\prime}\log fdx$
$\displaystyle=-\int(f^{\prime})^{2}/fdx$
(184)
by partial integration. Combining these statements gives the claim.
∎
Following [25], we can write the isoperimetric inequality  $1/N(X)\leq\frac{J(X)}{2\pi e}$  as
$\displaystyle-H(X)$
$\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{J(X)}{2\pi e}\right)$
(185)
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{J(X)}{2\pi}\right)-\frac{1}{2}\ .$
(186)
In particular, using
$\log x\leq x-1$ , we get
$\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{J(X)}{2\pi e}\right)$
$\displaystyle=\log\left(\frac{J(X)\cdot A}{2\pi eA}\right)$
$\displaystyle=\log\frac{1}{2\pi eA}+\log(AJ(X))$
$\displaystyle\leq AJ(X)-2-\log 2\pi A\ ,$
(187)
for any  $A>0$ .
Using inequality (187), it is straightforward to show the following.
Theorem 9 (Fast convergence of the cOU semigroup [25]).
Let  $\{X_{t}\}_{t\geq 0}$  be of the form (177), i.e., a solution to the cOU process
with parameters  $\theta>0,\sigma>0$ .
Then
$\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}D(X_{t}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})$
$\displaystyle\leq-2\theta D(X_{0}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})\ .$
(188)
Note that because we are considering a semigroup, this result
immediately implies that
$\displaystyle D(X_{t}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})\leq e^{-2\theta t}D(X_{0}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})\qquad\textrm{ for all }t\geq 0\ .$
(189)
Also, this result is tight:
if  $X_{0}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2}_{X_{0}})$  is a centered Gaussian random variable with variance  $\sigma^{2}_{X_{0}}$ , then (177) implies  $X_{t}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma_{t}^{2})$  where the variance of  $X_{t}$  is
$\displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=e^{-2\theta t}\sigma^{2}_{X_{0}}+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2\theta}(1-e^{-2\theta t})\ .$
(190)
Inserting into (179), using  $H(X_{t})=\frac{1}{2}(1+\log(2\pi\sigma_{t}^{2}))$
yields
$\displaystyle D(X_{t}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})$
$\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}(1+\log(2\pi\sigma_{t}^{2}))+\frac{1}{2}\log\pi\sigma^{2}/\theta+\frac{\theta}{\sigma^{2}}\sigma_{t}^{2}\ .$
(191)
In particular, we obtain
$\displaystyle\lim_{\sigma_{X_{0}}^{2}\rightarrow\infty}\left(\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}D(X_{t}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})\right)/D(X_{0}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})=-2\theta\ .$
(192)
Proof.
According to Eqs. (178), (179) and (180), we have
$\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}D(X_{t}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})$
$\displaystyle=-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}J(X_{0})-\frac{2\theta^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\mathbb{E}[X^{2}]+2\theta\ .$
(193)
Combining (187) with (179)
yields
$\displaystyle D(X_{0}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})\leq\frac{AJ(X)}{2}-(1+\frac{1}{2}\log 2\pi A)+\frac{1}{2}\log\pi\sigma^{2}/\theta+\theta/\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}[X_{0}^{2}]\ .$
(194)
Combining (194) with (193)
yields
$\displaystyle-2\theta D(X_{0}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})-\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}D(X_{t}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)})$
$\displaystyle\geq\left(-\theta A+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\right)J(X_{0})$
(195)
$\displaystyle+2\theta\left[\left(1+\frac{1}{2}\log 2\pi A-\frac{1}{2}\log\pi\sigma^{2}/\theta\right)-1\right]\ .$
(196)
The claim then follows by choosing  $A=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2\theta}$ .
∎
Appendix B Tightness of the quantum Fisher information isoperimetric inequality
Consider a one-mode Gaussian thermal state  $\omega_{\bf n}$  with mean photon number  ${\bf n}>0$ . Its entropy is
$\displaystyle S(\omega_{\bf n})$
$\displaystyle=g({\bf n})=({\bf n}+1)\log({\bf n}+1)-{\bf n}\log{\bf n}\ .$
(197)
Under the diffusion semigroup, the state  $\omega_{\bf n}$  evolves as
$\displaystyle e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathsf{heat}}}(\omega_{\bf n})$
$\displaystyle=\omega_{{\bf n}_{t}}\ ,\qquad\textrm{ where }\qquad{\bf n}_{t}={\bf n}+2\pi t\ .$
In particular, by the de Bruijn identity
$\displaystyle J(\omega_{\bf n})=2\,\frac{d}{dt}S(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathsf{heat}}}(\omega_{\bf n}))\bigg|_{t=0}=2g^{\prime}({\bf n}){\bf n}^{\prime}_{t}\Big|_{t=0}=4\pi\log\left(\frac{{\bf n}+1}{{\bf n}}\right)\ .$
(198)
Also,
$\displaystyle J(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathsf{heat}}}(\omega_{\bf n}))=4\pi\log\left(1+\frac{1}{{\bf n}+2\pi t}\right)\ .$
(199)
Calculating the right-hand side of the quantum Fisher information isoperimetric inequality (74), we obtain
$\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}\Bigl[\frac{1}{2}J(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathsf{heat}}}(\omega_{\bf n}))\Bigr]^{-1}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{{\bf n}({\bf n}+1)}\log^{-2}\left(1+\frac{1}{{\bf n}}\right)\rightarrow\ 1\qquad\text{ as }{\bf n}\rightarrow\infty\ .$
(200)
Appendix C Tightness of the isoperimetric inequality
Consider a one-mode Gaussian thermal state  $\omega_{\bf n}$  with mean photon number  ${\bf n}$ . From Eq. (198) we know that
$\displaystyle J(\omega_{\bf n})=4\pi\log\left(\frac{{\bf n}+1}{{\bf n}}\right)\ ,$
(201)
and that the entropy power of  $\omega_{\bf n}$  is given by (cf. (197))
$\displaystyle N(\omega_{\bf n})=\exp(S(\omega_{\bf n})/1)=\frac{({\bf n}+1)^{{\bf n}+1}}{{\bf n}^{\bf n}}\ .$
(202)
Combining these two expressions, we see that the left-hand side of (115) is
$\displaystyle J(\omega_{\bf n})N(\omega_{\bf n})=4\pi\left(\frac{{\bf n}+1}{{\bf n}}\right)^{{\bf n}}\log\left(\frac{{\bf n}+1}{{\bf n}}\right)^{{\bf n}+1}{\rightarrow}\ 4\pi e\qquad\text{ for }{{\bf n}\rightarrow\infty}\ .$
(203)
Appendix D On the convergence rate for Gaussian initial states
In this section we show that for a one-mode Gaussian state  $\rho$  the following inequality holds:
$\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}D(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mu,\lambda}}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\leq-\zeta D(\rho||\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\qquad$
$\displaystyle\text{ with }\zeta=\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}>0\ .$
(204)
Furthermore, this statement is optimal: for any  $\epsilon>0$  there exists a Gaussian state  $\rho$  such that
$\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}D(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mu,\lambda}}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\geq-(\zeta+\epsilon)D(\rho||\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\ .$
(205)
First, we note that the entropy of a Gaussian state does not depend on its first moments. Hence it follows that for a Gaussian state the right-hand side of Eq. (151) does not depend on its first moments, and it is suffices to consider centered Gaussian states.
Calculating the right-hand side of (151), we focus on calculating  $J_{\pm}(\rho)$ . Recall that the covariance matrix  $M$  of a centered state  $\rho$  is defined as  $M_{jk}=\mathsf{tr}(\rho\{R_{j},R_{k}\})$ .
Lemma 11.
Let  $\rho$  be a one-mode centered Gaussian state with mean-photon number  ${\bf n}$  and covariance matrix given by  $M=\kappa S^{T}S$ , where  $\kappa=2{\bf n}+1$ , and  $S=O_{1}\begin{pmatrix}z&0\\
0&1/z\end{pmatrix}O_{2}^{T}$  with  $O_{i}\in Sp(2)\cap O(2)$  and  $z\geq 1$ . Denote
$\left.J_{\pm}(\rho)=2\frac{d}{dt}S\left(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\pm}}(\rho)\right)\right|_{t=0}\ .$
Then we have
$J_{\pm}(\rho)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(1/z^{2}+z^{2}\right)\pm\kappa\right)\left(\log\left(\frac{\kappa+1}{2}\right)-\log\left(\frac{\kappa-1}{2}\right)\right)\ .$
(206)
Proof.
The covariance matrix of the time-evolved state  $e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\pm}}(\rho)$  is
$M_{\pm}(t)=c_{1}^{\pm}(t)M(0)+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)\mathop{\rm id}\ ,$
(207)
where
$\displaystyle c_{1}^{-}(t)=e^{-t}\qquad$
$\displaystyle\text{ and }\qquad c_{2}^{-}(t)=1-e^{-t}\ ,$
(208)
$\displaystyle c_{1}^{+}(t)=e^{t}\qquad$
$\displaystyle\text{ and }\qquad c_{2}^{+}(t)=e^{t}-1\ .$
(209)
Therefore writing  $S[M]$  for the entropy of a Gaussian state with covariance matrix  $M$ , we have
$\displaystyle S\left[M_{\pm}(t)\right]$
$\displaystyle=S\left[c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa S^{T}S+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)\mathop{\rm id}\right]=S\left[c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa O_{2}^{T}K^{T}O_{1}^{T}O_{1}KO_{2}+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)O_{2}^{T}O_{2}\right]$
(210)
$\displaystyle=S\left[c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa K^{T}O_{1}^{T}O_{1}K+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)\mathop{\rm id}\right]$
(211)
$\displaystyle=S\left[\begin{pmatrix}c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa z^{2}+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)&0\\
0&c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa/z^{2}+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)\end{pmatrix}\right]\ .$
(212)
The symplectic eigenvalue of the matrix argument in (212) is the square root of its determinant:
$\kappa_{\pm}(t)=\sqrt{\left(c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)z^{2}\right)\left(c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)/z^{2}\right)}\ .$
(213)
The entropy of the time evolved state is
$S(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\pm}}(\rho))=g({\bf n}(\kappa_{\pm}(t)))\ ,$
(214)
where  $g(x)=(x+1)\log(x+1)-x\log x$  and  ${\bf n}(\kappa)=\frac{1}{2}(\kappa-1)$ . By the chain rule, we have that
$\frac{d}{dt}S\left(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\pm}}(\rho)\right)=\frac{1}{2}g^{\prime}({\bf n}(\kappa_{\pm}(t)))\,{\kappa_{\pm}}^{\prime}(t)\ .$
(215)
Since  $g^{\prime}(x)=\log(x+1)-\log x$ , we only need to find  ${\kappa_{\pm}}^{\prime}(t)$ .
Combining (213) and (208) we obtain
$\displaystyle\kappa_{-}(t)$
$\displaystyle=\sqrt{\left(e^{-t}\kappa+\left(1-e^{-t}\right)z^{2}\right)\left(e^{-t}\kappa+\left(1-e^{-t}\right)/z^{2}\right)}$
(216)
$\displaystyle=\kappa+t\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(z^{2}+1/z^{2}\right)-\kappa\right)+O\left(t^{2}\right)\ .$
(217)
Therefore  $\left.{\kappa_{-}}^{\prime}(t)\right|_{t=0}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1/z^{2}+z^{2}\right)-\kappa$  and finally
$J_{-}(\rho)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(1/z^{2}+z^{2}\right)-\kappa\right)\log\frac{\kappa+1}{\kappa-1}\ .$
(218)
Similarly, using (213) together with (209), we obtain
$\displaystyle\kappa_{+}(t)$
$\displaystyle=\sqrt{\left(e^{t}\kappa+\left(e^{t}-1\right)z^{2}\right)\left(e^{t}\kappa+\left(e^{t}-1\right)/z^{2}\right)}$
(219)
$\displaystyle=\kappa+t\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(z^{2}+1/z^{2}\right)+\kappa\right)+O\left(t^{2}\right)\ .$
(220)
Thus  $\left.{\kappa_{+}}^{\prime}(t)\right|_{t=0}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1/z^{2}+z^{2}\right)+\kappa$  and
$J_{+}(\rho)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(1/z^{2}+z^{2}\right)+\kappa\right)\log\frac{\kappa+1}{\kappa-1}\ .$
(221)
∎
From Lemma 8 it is clear that we are interested in minimizing  $J_{\pm}(\rho)$ . Both expressions in (206) have a minimum at  $z=1$ . Therefore, with  $\zeta=\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}$  and  ${\bf n}=\frac{\kappa-1}{2}$ , from Lemma 8 we obtain
$\displaystyle-\zeta D(\rho||\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})-\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}D(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mu,\lambda}}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\geq$
$\displaystyle\mu^{2}\log({\bf n}+1)-\lambda^{2}\log{\bf n}+\lambda^{2}\log\lambda^{2}$
(222)
$\displaystyle-\mu^{2}\log\mu^{2}+(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})\log(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})$
(223)
$\displaystyle=:$
$\displaystyle h_{\mu,\lambda}({\bf n})\ .$
(224)
For fixed  $\mu^{2}>\lambda^{2}$ , the function  $h_{\mu,\lambda}$  satisfies  $\lim_{{\bf n}\rightarrow 0}h_{\mu,\lambda}({\bf n})=\lim_{{\bf n}\rightarrow\infty}h_{\mu,\lambda}({\bf n})=\infty$ . Since  $h_{\mu,\lambda}$  is differentiable (in fact smooth) for  ${\bf n}>0$ , we can find the global minimum by finding the zeros of the derivative
$\displaystyle\frac{d}{d{\bf n}}h_{\mu,\lambda}({\bf n})=\frac{\mu^{2}}{{\bf n}+1}-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{{\bf n}}=0\ .$
(225)
The only solution is  ${\bf n}=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}}$ , and since
$\displaystyle\frac{d^{2}}{d{\bf n}^{2}}\bigg|_{{\bf n}=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}}}h_{\mu,\lambda}({\bf n})=(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})\left(\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}}-\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\right)>0\ ,$
(226)
it is the minimum. The value of the minimum is  $h_{\mu,\lambda}\left(\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}}\right)=0$ , hence it follows that  $h_{\mu,\lambda}({\bf n})\geq 0$  for all  ${\bf n}>0$  and we have
$\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}D(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mu,\lambda}}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\leq-\zeta D(\rho\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\ .$
(227)
Moreover, the last inequality becomes equality for  $\rho=\sigma_{\mu,\lambda}=\omega_{{\bf n}_{\infty}}$ , with  ${\bf n}_{\infty}=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}}$ .
It remains to show that  $\zeta=\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}$  is optimal. Let  $\epsilon>0$  and  $\zeta^{\prime}=\zeta+\epsilon$ . Then for the Gaussian thermal state  $\omega_{\bf n}$  we have
$\displaystyle-\zeta^{\prime}D(\omega_{\bf n}\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})-\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}D(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mu,\lambda}}(\omega_{\bf n})\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})=$
$\displaystyle h_{\mu,\lambda}({\bf n})+\epsilon({\bf n}+1)\log({\bf n}+1)-\epsilon\,{\bf n}\log{\bf n}$
(228)
$\displaystyle+\epsilon\,{\bf n}\log\left(\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)+\epsilon\log\left(1-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)$
(229)
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\log\left(\left(\frac{{\bf n}+1}{{\bf n}}\right)^{\mu^{2}+\epsilon({\bf n}+1)}{\bf n}^{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}+\epsilon}\left(\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)^{\epsilon{\bf n}}\right)$
(230)
$\displaystyle+\mathrm{c}(\mu,\lambda)\ {\rightarrow}-\infty\qquad\text{ for }{{\bf n}\rightarrow\infty}\ ,$
(231)
where  $\mathrm{c}(\mu,\lambda)=\log\left((\mu^{2})^{-\mu^{2}-\epsilon}(\lambda^{2})^{\lambda^{2}}(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})^{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}+\epsilon}\right)$ .
Therefore, for any  $\epsilon>0$ , there exists  ${\bf n}$  such that
$\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}D(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mu,\lambda}}(\omega_{\bf n})\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})>-(\zeta+\epsilon)D(\omega_{\bf n}||\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\ .$
(232)
This shows that the constant  $\zeta=\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}$  is optimal in the inequality (204).

Instructions for reporting errors
We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
methods listed below:
Click the "Report Issue" (
) button, located in the page header.
Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.
Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
all.
Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
We gratefully acknowledge support from
our major funders,
member institutions, ,
and all contributors.
